name: Winter ferry schedule
publisher: Department of Marine and Ports Services
how: Typed in from the published brochure and checked against it twice. This file is kept by hand: replace the tables when Marine and Ports publishes a new schedule, and move review_after on. Times are 24 hour. An empty string means the ferry does not call there on that run.

routes.name: Blue Route
routes.note: Motorcycles allowed. The crossing takes about 20 minutes.

routes.name: Green Route
routes.line: Hamilton, Watford Bridge, Cavello Bay and Rockaway
routes.note: Monday to Friday only. No motorcycles at Watford Bridge or Cavello Bay. Morning runs call at Watford Bridge first, evening runs at Rockaway first.

routes.name: Pink Route
routes.note: Weekdays only. No motorcycles. Morning runs call at Belmont first, afternoon runs at Salt Kettle first.

routes.name: Orange Route
routes.note: No service on the Orange Route this winter.

history_source: From The Bermudian magazine's history of the ferry boats, rewritten in our own words.
history: A pound of tobacco
The first ferry keeper was appointed in 1622, for the crossing between Coney Island and Ferry Island at the east end. He rowed, and lived on what passengers chose to give.
An act of 1627 fixed his fee at a pound of tobacco from everyone over 16 and gave the ferry its own land. He worked every day but Sunday.
A barge for horses and carriages was added in the 1790s. On one day in January 1847 it carried about 750 people, 58 horses and 24 carriages to the races in St George's.
The Causeway opened in 1871 and put the ferry out of work, until a gale wrecked the bridge in 1899 and it was needed again.
Sail and steam
In 1784 a sailing boat began carrying the mail twice a week from Salt Kettle to St George's. A letter cost fourpence.
The first steam ferry, the Express, ran from Salt Kettle in 1867. In the 1870s the steamers Reliance and Dispatch linked Hamilton and the Dockyard.
The Daisy began crossing from St George's to St David's on 15 October 1895, every two hours, with room for about 60.
Watford Bridge opened in 1903 and ended the horse ferry there. In 1911 the Bermuda Transportation Company took over and brought in motor ferries.
Boats people remember
Corona began life about 1892 as a Hudson River ferry. She carried 350 passengers between Hamilton and Somerset and lasted more than fifty years.

Laconia worked the Paget and Warwick route for forty years, carried an estimated eight million passengers and travelled more than a million miles before she was scuttled in 1963. Her successor lies derelict in Ely's Harbour.
Coralita, built in Maine in 1914, ran to Somerset until 1963.
Wilhelmina, once a private yacht, caught fire near Watford Bridge in 1955. One passenger died and 58 were saved.
Dragon, a former army minesweeper, blew up off the ferry terminal in 1953, was rebuilt, and ran until 1967.
Each week the old steamers called at the reservoir on Hawkins Island to take on 15 to 20 tons of water for their boilers.
The last man who rowed
Walter Hilgrove Ingham bought a rowing boat for 12 pounds in 1912 and rowed passengers across Hamilton Harbour for forty years, first for a penny ha'penny and later for twopence.
He was killed on 31 March 1952 when he was drawn into the propeller of a large ship. The rowing ferry ended with him.
Fast ferries
The fast catamarans arrived in 2002 and cut the run from Hamilton to Dockyard to about 20 minutes. One is named for Cecil Smith, a pilot who joined the ferry company in 1925.
